vo.text: [softly] Right now, somewhere on Earth, a river is rising.
The ground is cracking. A forest is thinning. A glacier is slipping toward the sea.
[softly] Our planet never stops moving, and most of it happens where no one is looking.
We are The L Band. We named ourselves after the radar band that lets NISAR see through clouds, because that's exactly what we wanted to do.
মোহাম্মদ গোলাম ফারুক অভি leads the team as system and solution architect.
এম ডি জাহারাবি ভূঁইয়া রাফি shapes the product as our product analyst.
মোহাম্মদ মুশফিক উস সালেহীন builds the intelligence as our AI engineer.
রেজাউল করিম অনিক digs into the science as our system researcher.
And রিফাহ তামান্না keeps us all connected, leading communication and coordination.
[warmly] We come from a country that lives with water. So this challenge didn't feel like homework. It felt like home.
Meet NISAR, a satellite built by NASA and ISRO together.
It carries a radar that brings its own light. Day or night, through cloud and storm, it keeps watching.
Every twelve days, it comes back to map nearly all of Earth's land and ice.
What you're seeing is its real orbit, replayed over Bangladesh on September twenty-second.
In just three days, it captured more than two thousand images.
[quietly] But there's a catch.
Open a single image, and this is what you get: nearly seven gigabytes of radar data, made for specialists.
The floods, the earthquakes, the failing crops are all in there. But for the people who need them most, they stay invisible.
So we built Earth Pulse: a way to see what the radar sees.
This is Bangladesh, through NISAR's eyes. Calm water turns radar away, so water shows up dark.
Now watch, twelve days at a time, as the river spills across its floodplain.
June on one side. July on the other.
Nearly two thousand square kilometres became water-like. That's an estimate we compute, and we label it honestly as one.
Now, Japan. Five radar views of the same place, stacked through time.
On July twenty-eighth, a magnitude six-point-eight earthquake struck Kumamoto. Only one of these pairs spans that moment…
…and only that one lights up. Tight rings, right on the epicentre.
Each ring traces the ground itself, moving toward or away from the satellite.
The ground moved, and NISAR saw it from orbit.
But we didn't want five stories. We wanted every place on Earth.
So: click anywhere. Earth Pulse finds two NISAR passes of that exact spot…
…lines them up, and shows you what changed, live, in your browser.
Every pixel has a source. Every claim tells you how sure we are. And nothing simulated ever pretends to be real.
[hushed] This challenge is called Dancing with the SARs, so we made the change dance. Listen.
Picture a farmer checking a flooded field after a night of rain. A rescue team asking where the water went. A student watching an earthquake reshape the ground.
Next, we'll bring in calibrated NISAR measurements, change alerts for any place on Earth, and ISRO's S-band radar to help explain every change.
We can't do it alone. We need Earthdata access and compute, mentors in radar science, and partners on the ground in disaster response.
[softly] Because one day, anyone, anywhere, should be able to ask: what changed here?
[warmly] We are The L Band. This is Earth Pulse. Watch Earth change.
